title: Santa Claus Conquers the Martians

evidence.note: Renewal absence cannot make this 1964 film public domain. For a work first published in 1964, 17 U.S.C. 304(a)(3)(B) says a renewal application 'is not a condition of the renewal and extension of the copyright', so the renewal term attaches automatically. Public domain would have to rest on a missing copyright notice on the 1964 release prints, and I could not verify that from any source I fetched. Wikipedia says the film is in the public domain in the United States but does not document the basis.

Sound film with a score by Milton DeLugg (per Wikipedia). The recorded soundtrack normally shares the film's status, so it is undetermined for the same reason as the print. I did not verify any separate music copyright or registration.

Wikipedia credits Paul L. Jacobson and Glenville Mareth with the story and screenplay. I found no separate publication or registration of the story, so the story layer follows the print and is undetermined.

Plagiarism Today says the film is public domain only in the United States, and that elsewhere STUDIOCANAL holds the copyright and enforces it. I did not confirm any specific restoration or its added material. Any cleaned-up transfer, new titles or added commentary would be protectable even if the underlying print were free.

editorial:
Santa Claus Conquers the Martians is a 1964 American Christmas science-fiction comedy directed by Nicholas Webster, with Paul L. Jacobson as producer, John Call as Santa Claus and Pia Zadora as the Martian child Girmar. Milton DeLugg composed the score. It was shot in color over two weeks in July and August 1964 at Michael Myerberg Studios on Long Island, and Embassy Pictures released it on November 14, 1964. The budget is estimated at $200,000. It became a cult title and was featured on Mystery Science Theater 3000, which is why a creator might want clips of it.

The rights trap is the shortcut that an old film was never renewed. A film published in 1964 got its renewal term automatically under 17 U.S.C. 304(a), so renewal does not decide this one. It would have to be free for another reason, such as a missing notice, and I found no document establishing that. Wikipedia and the Internet Archive metadata call it public domain in the US, but neither documents the basis. Plagiarism Today says it is public domain only in the US and that STUDIOCANAL holds and enforces the copyright elsewhere. Check the notice on an actual print before reusing it, and keep it out of non-US distribution.
faq: Is Santa Claus Conquers the Martians public domain because the copyright was not renewed?

That reason does not work for a 1964 film. Under 17 U.S.C. 304(a)(3)(B) a renewal application is not a condition of the renewal term, so the term attaches automatically. The film could be public domain in the US only through a defect such as a missing copyright notice. I could not verify one, so the status is undetermined here.
Can I use the Internet Archive copy, including outside the US?

The Internet Archive copy is a community upload carrying a Public Domain Mark in its metadata; I have not verified its source or quality beyond that. Plagiarism Today reports that outside the US, STUDIOCANAL holds and enforces the copyright. For anything beyond US use, get a clearance first.
